paragraphes: Your phone knows your name, your voice, your photos, and the places you go. All of this is about you.
Imagine an app sells it to strangers and does not tell you. Nobody broke into anything. But it feels unfair.
That feeling has a name. You lost control of your privacy.

decouverte.comme: Your diary is about you. Only you decide who can read it.
decouverte.enVrai: Privacy is confidentiality for personal data. Personal data is information about one person. It is also called PII, short for personally identifiable information. The image stops here. You keep your diary at home, but a company often keeps your data. Laws make that company protect it.

decouverte.question: A company keeps the addresses of its customers. Who must protect these addresses?
options: Only the customers themselves
The company, because laws say so
Nobody, because addresses are public
decouverte.answer: The company, because laws say so
decouverte.explanation: Customers cannot protect data that they do not keep. The company keeps it, so the laws give the company this duty.

decouverte.texte: You buy sneakers online. The site asks for your name, your address, and your birth date. These are PII. A law may force the shop to protect them. It may also force the shop to tell you how it uses them.

decouverte.comme: Each country has its own traffic rules. When you drive abroad, you follow the rules of that country.
decouverte.enVrai: Privacy laws work the same way. Each country or region has its own laws. A jurisdiction is the area where a law applies. A security professional must know the laws of their jurisdiction.

cards.question: Official definition: “privacy”
cards.answer: As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of confidentiality applied to personal data.
cards.explanation: In simple words: privacy is confidentiality, but only for data about people.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “privacy”?
options: As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of integrity applied to personal data.
As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of confidentiality applied to all company data.
As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of confidentiality applied to personal data.
As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of availability applied to personal data.
options_why: It uses integrity. Integrity is about keeping data correct, not secret.
Privacy is about personal data only, not about all company data.
It uses availability. Availability is about reaching data when you need it.
cards.answer: As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of confidentiality applied to personal data.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: security principle of confidentiality, applied to personal data.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “privacy” from memory.
cards.answer: As discussed earlier in this chapter, privacy is effectively the security principle of confidentiality applied to personal data.
cards.explanation: Three parts: privacy is, in practice, the principle of confidentiality, applied to personal data.

cards.question: Official definition: the “APEC Privacy Framework”
cards.answer: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Privacy Framework is intended to provide member nations and economies with a flexible and consistent approach to information privacy protection without unnecessarily stifling information flow.
cards.explanation: A framework gives shared ideas to many countries. It is not a law. It helps data move between countries.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”. The manual says that it is not a law or regulation.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “APEC Privacy Framework” from memory.
cards.answer: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Privacy Framework is intended to provide member nations and economies with a flexible and consistent approach to information privacy protection without unnecessarily stifling information flow.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: a flexible and consistent approach, privacy protection, and no needless block on information flow.

cards.question: A website shows the home addresses of its customers to the public by mistake. Which idea is hit first?
options: Integrity, because the addresses were changed
Privacy, because private data was shown to others
Availability, because the site stopped working
Nothing, because home addresses are public information
options_why: Nobody changed the addresses. They are still correct.
The site still works. The problem is who can see the data.
A home address is PII. It is not public by default.
cards.answer: Privacy, because private data was shown to others
cards.explanation: The addresses did not change, but people who should not see them can see them. That is confidentiality of personal data.

cards.question: What is privacy, in simple words?
options: Integrity for all company data
Availability of personal data
One privacy law that all countries share
Confidentiality for personal data
options_why: Integrity is about correct data. Privacy is about personal data only.
Availability is about reaching data. Privacy is about who can see it.
Privacy is an idea. The laws are different in each place.
cards.answer: Confidentiality for personal data
cards.explanation: Privacy is the part of confidentiality that protects data about people.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”.

cards.question: Which of these is PII?
options: A customer's birth date
The price of a product
The number of customers in a shop
The name of a software tool
options_why: A price does not point to one person.
A total does not point to one person.
A tool name does not point to one person.
cards.answer: A customer's birth date
cards.explanation: PII is data that can point to one exact person, like a name or a birth date.

cards.question: Which statement about privacy and security is true?
options: Privacy makes security controls unnecessary
Security is only about hardware, and privacy only about people
Security starts only after a privacy law is broken
Privacy needs security to protect personal data
options_why: Without security, personal data cannot be kept private.
Security protects data of all kinds, and it supports privacy.
Security works before a problem, to stop it.
cards.answer: Privacy needs security to protect personal data
cards.explanation: The manual says that privacy and information security go hand in hand.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, first sentence of the section “Privacy”.

cards.question: Camille works for a company that has customers in several countries. What should she look at FIRST to know which privacy laws apply?
options: The jurisdictions of the company and of its customers
Only the country where the servers are
Only the rules inside the company
The newest law in the world, because it replaces the others
options_why: Laws often follow the people concerned, not only the machines.
Internal rules never replace the law.
Laws apply by jurisdiction. A new law elsewhere does not replace them.
cards.answer: The jurisdictions of the company and of its customers
cards.explanation: Each law applies in its own jurisdiction. A security professional must know the laws that touch the company and its customers.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”: understand each privacy regulation that governs your jurisdiction.

cards.question: A company protects its files well against hackers. But it sells customer data and does not tell the customers. What is the BEST description?
options: Privacy is respected, because the files are safe and protected from hackers
The files are safe, but the privacy of the customers is not respected
Privacy is respected, because no customer complained
Only availability is lost, because the files are used by others
options_why: Good security is not enough. The company also decides who sees the data and why.
Silence is not consent. The customers did not even know.
The files still work. The problem is who can see the data.
cards.answer: The files are safe, but the privacy of the customers is not respected
cards.explanation: Privacy is about who may see personal data and for what reason. Strong security alone does not give that.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT personal data (PII)?
options: A student's name
A person's social security number
The total number of customers of a shop
A customer's birth date
options_why: A name points to one person, so it is PII.
This number points to one exact person, so it is PII.
A birth date helps to identify one person, so it is PII.
cards.answer: The total number of customers of a shop
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: does this information help me to recognize one exact person? A total does not.

cards.question: Which task is MOST closely linked to privacy?
options: Making a server run faster
Deciding who may see customer addresses, and why
Testing a backup of the company files
Fixing a typing mistake in a price list
options_why: Speed is not about personal data.
Backups are about availability, not about who sees personal data.
A price is not personal data, and this is about correctness.
cards.answer: Deciding who may see customer addresses, and why
cards.explanation: Privacy is about control over personal data: who sees it and for what reason.

cards.question: Which statement about the APEC Privacy Framework is correct?
options: It is a law that all APEC countries must follow
It is a privacy regulation of the European Union
It stops information from moving between countries
It is not a law, but it gives shared privacy ideas
options_why: The manual says that it is not a law or a regulation.
APEC is the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, not the EU.
Its aim is to avoid stopping the flow of information without a good reason.
cards.answer: It is not a law, but it gives shared privacy ideas
cards.explanation: The framework helps countries to agree on a common set of privacy ideas, without forcing them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on the APEC Privacy Framework.

cards.question: A company opens an online shop. Which step is BEST for respecting the privacy of its customers?
options: Tell them what data is collected, and protect it from unauthorized access
Collect all the data that it can, in case it is useful later
Protect the data well, but tell the customers nothing
Ask each customer to protect their own data
options_why: Collecting more than needed adds risk and does not respect privacy.
Customers should know how their data is used.
Customers cannot protect data that the company keeps.
cards.answer: Tell them what data is collected, and protect it from unauthorized access
cards.explanation: Privacy needs two things: being open with the person, and protecting the data.

cards.question: What is privacy, in one sentence?
cards.answer: Privacy is confidentiality applied to personal data.
cards.explanation: Think of your diary: it is about you, and you decide who reads it.

cards.question: What does PII stand for?
cards.answer: Personally identifiable information. It is data that can point to one exact person.
cards.explanation: Think of a name, a birth date, or a social security number.

cards.question: Is the APEC Privacy Framework a law?
cards.answer: No. It is not a law or a regulation. It is a set of shared privacy ideas.
cards.explanation: It helps countries of one region to agree, without forcing them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on the APEC Privacy Framework.

cards.question: Why must a security professional know the privacy laws of their jurisdiction?
cards.answer: Because each place has its own laws, and the professional must follow the ones that apply.
cards.explanation: The same data can follow different rules in different places.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”.

concepts.name: US laws: the government, children and banks

paragraphes: Your name is in a government file. It is also on a game site, and at your parents' bank.
Each place keeps information about you. The risks are not the same. So the rules are not the same.
In the United States, there is one law for each sector. You will meet the laws for the government, for children online, and for banks.

decouverte.comme: At school, the library, the gym, and the cafeteria each have their own rules. Each place has its own risks.
decouverte.enVrai: In the United States, many laws share the work of protecting privacy. Each law is for one sector. One is for government offices, one is for children online, and one is for banks.

decouverte.question: A game site collects data from 10-year-old children. Which US law should you check FIRST?
options: The law that protects children online
The law that protects bank customers
The law that governs government files
decouverte.answer: The law that protects children online
decouverte.explanation: The other two laws are about other sectors. The law for children online is called COPPA. It covers children under 13.

decouverte.texte: Leo is 11. He wants an account on a US game site. The site must first get his parents' agreement. This is also called consent. The law COPPA asks for this. It protects children under 13.

decouverte.titre: The label on a cookie pack
decouverte.comme: The label on a pack tells you what is inside. You know what you eat before you buy.
decouverte.enVrai: A bank must do the same with your data. It gives you a written notice. The notice says what data the bank collects, how it uses the data, and how it protects the data.

cards.question: Official definition: the US “Privacy Act”
cards.answer: The Privacy Act establishes and governs practices related to the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of PII by U.S. government agencies.
cards.explanation: In simple words: this law is about the government. It says how government offices must handle personal data.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Federal Privacy Act of 1974”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the US “Privacy Act”?
options: The Privacy Act establishes and governs practices related to the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of PII by U.S. private companies.
The Privacy Act establishes and governs practices related to the collection and storage of PII by U.S. government agencies.
The Privacy Act establishes and governs practices related to the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of PII by U.S. government agencies.
The Privacy Act forbids the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of PII by U.S. government agencies.
options_why: It changes government agencies to private companies. The act is about the government.
It lists only collection and storage. The real sentence has four stages.
The act governs these practices. It does not forbid all of them.
cards.answer: The Privacy Act establishes and governs practices related to the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of PII by U.S. government agencies.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination, and U.S. government agencies.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the US “Privacy Act” from memory.
cards.answer: The Privacy Act establishes and governs practices related to the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of PII by U.S. government agencies.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the name of the law, the four stages of data (collection, maintenance, use, dissemination), and government agencies.

cards.question: Official definition: the purpose of the Privacy Act
cards.answer: The purpose of the Privacy Act is to balance the government's need to maintain information about citizens and permanent residents with the rights of those individuals to keep their personal information private.
cards.explanation: The key word is balance. The government needs data, but people have the right to keep their data private.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Federal Privacy Act of 1974”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the purpose of the Privacy Act from memory.
cards.answer: The purpose of the Privacy Act is to balance the government's need to maintain information about citizens and permanent residents with the rights of those individuals to keep their personal information private.
cards.explanation: Remember the word balance, and its two sides: the needs of the government and the rights of the people.

cards.question: Official definition: “COPPA”
cards.answer: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for online businesses to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13.
cards.explanation: COPPA means: children, online, under 13.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998”. The manual adds that COPPA applies to any organization that handles data of children living in the United States.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “COPPA”?
options: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for online businesses to protect the privacy of children under the age of 18.
The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1999 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for online businesses to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13.
The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for schools to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13.
The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for online businesses to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13.
options_why: The age is 18 here. The real age is 13.
The year is wrong. COPPA is from 1998. The year 1999 is for GLBA.
It changes online businesses to schools.
cards.answer: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for online businesses to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: 1998, strict guidelines, online businesses, and children under the age of 13.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “COPPA” from memory.
cards.answer: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 is a U.S. federal law that establishes strict guidelines for online businesses to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13.
cards.explanation: Strict rules, for online businesses, about children under 13.

cards.question: Official definition: the “GLBA” law
cards.answer: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1999, is a U.S. law that requires financial institutions to safeguard their customer's PII.
cards.explanation: GLBA is about banks and similar companies. They must protect the data of their customers.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “GLBA” law?
options: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1999, is a U.S. law that requires financial institutions to safeguard their customer's PII.
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1999, is a U.S. law that requires financial institutions to publish their customer's PII.
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1974, is a U.S. law that requires financial institutions to safeguard their customer's PII.
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1999, is a U.S. law that requires government agencies to safeguard their customer's PII.
options_why: It says publish. The real word is safeguard, which is the opposite.
The year is wrong. GLBA is from 1999. The year 1974 is for the Privacy Act.
It changes financial institutions to government agencies.
cards.answer: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1999, is a U.S. law that requires financial institutions to safeguard their customer's PII.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: Financial Services Modernization Act, financial institutions, and safeguard.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “GLBA” law from memory.
cards.answer: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, also known as the Financial Services Modernization Act of 1999, is a U.S. law that requires financial institutions to safeguard their customer's PII.
cards.explanation: Another name for the law, the institutions it covers, and what they must do: safeguard PII.

cards.question: Official definition: the GLBA “Financial Privacy Rule”
cards.answer: Among the provisions within GLBA, the Financial Privacy Rule requires that financial institutions provide each customer with a written privacy notice that explains what personal information is collected from the customer, how it is used, and how it is protected.
cards.explanation: Think of the label on a pack. The bank tells the customer in writing what it collects, how it uses it, and how it protects it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the GLBA “Financial Privacy Rule” from memory.
cards.answer: Among the provisions within GLBA, the Financial Privacy Rule requires that financial institutions provide each customer with a written privacy notice that explains what personal information is collected from the customer, how it is used, and how it is protected.
cards.explanation: Three parts: a written privacy notice, then what is collected and how it is used, and how it is protected.

cards.question: Official definition: the GLBA “Safeguards Rule”
cards.answer: The GLBA Safeguards Rule requires organizations to implement proper security controls to protect their customers' personal data.
cards.explanation: One rule tells the customer (Financial Privacy Rule). This rule protects the data (Safeguards Rule).
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the GLBA “Safeguards Rule” from memory.
cards.answer: The GLBA Safeguards Rule requires organizations to implement proper security controls to protect their customers' personal data.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the name of the rule, who must act (organizations), and what they must put in place (proper security controls).

cards.question: A bank gives each customer a written notice about how it uses their data. Which law asks for this?
options: COPPA
The Privacy Act
GLBA
No law, because banks decide alone
options_why: COPPA is about children under 13 online, not about banks.
The Privacy Act is about government agencies.
GLBA requires the notice. Banks do not decide alone.
cards.answer: GLBA
cards.explanation: GLBA is about financial institutions. Its Financial Privacy Rule asks for a written privacy notice.

cards.question: A game site wants to open accounts for 10-year-old children. Which law mostly applies?
options: GLBA, the law about banks
COPPA, the law about children online
The Privacy Act, the law about the government
No law, because the site is a private company
options_why: A game site is not a financial institution.
This law is about government agencies, not private sites.
COPPA is aimed at online businesses, so private companies are covered.
cards.answer: COPPA, the law about children online
cards.explanation: COPPA protects children under 13 online. Online businesses must follow its strict guidelines.

cards.question: Which group of people does COPPA protect?
options: Children under the age of 18
Customers of banks
Children under the age of 13
Citizens who are in government files
options_why: The age in the law is 13, not 18.
That is the sector of GLBA.
That is the sector of the Privacy Act.
cards.answer: Children under the age of 13
cards.explanation: COPPA is about the privacy of children under 13 who use online services.

cards.question: A US government agency wants to send a citizen's file to another agency. What must the agency get FIRST?
options: The agreement of the second agency only
A written request, or the prior written consent of the person
A message to the person, sent after the file is sent
Nothing, because agencies can share files freely
options_why: The agreement of the person matters. Two agencies cannot decide alone.
Consent must come before, not after.
The Privacy Act strongly limits these exchanges.
cards.answer: A written request, or the prior written consent of the person
cards.explanation: An agency must not share a record without a written request or the prior written consent (agreement) of the person.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Federal Privacy Act of 1974”. Today, online consent forms can count as written consent.

cards.question: What is the BEST way for a site to respect COPPA with children under 13?
options: Collect the data first and ask the parents later
Protect the data with encryption and do not contact the parents
Ask each child to promise that they are old enough
Get the agreement of the parents before collecting data
options_why: The agreement must come before the collection.
Encryption helps, but COPPA also asks for parental consent.
A promise from a child does not replace the parents' agreement.
cards.answer: Get the agreement of the parents before collecting data
cards.explanation: COPPA sets requirements for seeking parental consent, and limits on marketing to children under 13.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a duty that comes from GLBA?
options: Getting the parents' agreement for children under 13
Giving each customer a written privacy notice
Putting security controls in place for customer data
Safeguarding the PII of customers
options_why: This is the Financial Privacy Rule, which is part of GLBA.
This is the Safeguards Rule, which is part of GLBA.
This is the main duty of GLBA.
cards.answer: Getting the parents' agreement for children under 13
cards.explanation: Parental consent comes from COPPA, the law about children online. It is not a GLBA duty.

cards.question: Which organization MOST clearly needs to follow GLBA?
options: A game site for 10-year-old children
A federal agency that keeps files of citizens
A bank that keeps customer accounts and PII
A shop that sells shoes in the street
options_why: That site must look at COPPA.
That agency must look at the Privacy Act.
A shoe shop is not a financial institution.
cards.answer: A bank that keeps customer accounts and PII
cards.explanation: GLBA requires financial institutions to safeguard the PII of their customers.

cards.question: Which list puts these three laws in order, from the oldest to the newest?
options: COPPA, Privacy Act, and then GLBA
Privacy Act, COPPA, GLBA
GLBA, COPPA, and then Privacy Act
Privacy Act, GLBA, and then COPPA
options_why: The Privacy Act is from 1974, so it is the oldest.
This is the reverse order. GLBA is the newest, from 1999.
COPPA (1998) comes just before GLBA (1999).
cards.answer: Privacy Act, COPPA, GLBA
cards.explanation: The Privacy Act is from 1974, COPPA is from 1998, and GLBA is from 1999.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”.

cards.question: Which penalty can GLBA bring for an organization?
options: A civil fine of up to 100,000 dollars per violation
A fine of up to 43,280 dollars per violation
A fine of up to 5,000 dollars per violation
A fine of up to 1.5 million dollars per year
options_why: This amount is for COPPA.
This amount is for criminal violations of the Privacy Act.
This amount belongs to another law, not to GLBA.
cards.answer: A civil fine of up to 100,000 dollars per violation
cards.explanation: GLBA civil fines go up to 100,000 dollars per violation for an organization. For its officers and directors, they go up to 10,000 dollars.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999”.

cards.question: A bank wants to follow the GLBA Safeguards Rule. Which action is BEST?
options: Send customers a written notice and do nothing more
Stop collecting any customer data at all
Ask each customer to protect their own data
Put proper security controls in place to protect customer data
options_why: The notice is the Financial Privacy Rule. The Safeguards Rule asks for security controls.
This is extreme. The rule asks to protect the data, not to stop collecting it.
The bank holds the data, so the bank must protect it.
cards.answer: Put proper security controls in place to protect customer data
cards.explanation: The Safeguards Rule asks organizations to implement proper security controls to protect personal data of customers.

cards.question: What is the highest civil fine for one COPPA violation, according to the FTC?
cards.answer: Up to 43,280 dollars for each violation.
cards.explanation: The number is exact. Remember the words for each violation.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on COPPA. FTC means Federal Trade Commission.

cards.question: What penalty can a criminal violation of the Privacy Act bring?
cards.answer: It is a misdemeanor. The fine can be up to 5,000 dollars per violation.
cards.explanation: A misdemeanor is a less serious offense than a crime.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on the Privacy Act of 1974.

cards.question: What civil fines can GLBA bring?
cards.answer: Up to 100,000 dollars per violation for the organization, and up to 10,000 dollars for its officers and directors.
cards.explanation: Two amounts: a big one for the company, a smaller one for the people who run it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. Criminal violations can also lead to loss of licenses and up to five years in prison.

cards.question: In which years were the Privacy Act, COPPA, and GLBA made?
cards.answer: The Privacy Act in 1974, COPPA in 1998, and GLBA in 1999.
cards.explanation: Link each year to a sector: government, children, banks.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy”.

cards.question: What do the two GLBA rules ask for, in simple words?
cards.answer: The Financial Privacy Rule asks for a written notice to the customer. The Safeguards Rule asks for security controls.
cards.explanation: One rule is about telling the customer. The other is about protecting the data.

paragraphes: You go to the doctor. They write down your illness, your medicines, and your test results.
Imagine your insurer, your neighbor, or a future employer reads this file. It would be embarrassing. Sometimes it would be unfair.
In the United States, this data is called PHI, short for protected health information. A law protects it. The law is called HIPAA, short for Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act.

decouverte.comme: The doctor keeps your file in a locked drawer. Only people who must treat you or send the bill can see the pages.
decouverte.enVrai: The HIPAA Privacy Rule says who can see your health file and why. The Security Rule says how to lock the drawer when the file is on a computer. A disclosure is when the data is shown to someone.

decouverte.question: Who must follow the HIPAA law?
options: Only doctors
Insurers, caregivers, and billing services
Every company that has customers
decouverte.explanation: These are the three groups of covered entities. Doctors are only one part of them. A shoe shop is not covered.

decouverte.texte: Your family's health insurance is a health plan. The hospital is a healthcare provider. A company that changes the hospital's bills into a standard format for the insurer is a healthcare clearinghouse. All three must follow HIPAA.

cards.question: Official definition: “covered entities”
cards.answer: Organizations that must comply with HIPAA requirements are known as covered entities and fit into three categories:
cards.explanation: A covered entity is an organization that must follow HIPAA. There are three groups of them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “covered entities” from memory.
cards.answer: Organizations that must comply with HIPAA requirements are known as covered entities and fit into three categories:
cards.explanation: Three parts: who must comply with HIPAA, their name (covered entities), and the number of categories (three).

cards.question: Official definition: “health plans”
cards.answer: Health plans: This includes health insurance companies, government programs like Medicare, and military and veteran's health programs that pay for healthcare.
cards.explanation: A health plan is a group that pays for care. It can be an insurer or a government program.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”. Medicare is a US government health insurance program.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “health plans” from memory.
cards.answer: Health plans: This includes health insurance companies, government programs like Medicare, and military and veteran's health programs that pay for healthcare.
cards.explanation: Three kinds of payers: insurance companies, government programs like Medicare, and military and veteran's programs.

cards.question: Official definition: “healthcare providers”
cards.answer: Healthcare providers: This includes hospitals, doctors, nursing homes, pharmacies, and other medical providers that transmit health information.
cards.explanation: Healthcare providers give care and pass on health information.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “healthcare providers” from memory.
cards.answer: Healthcare providers: This includes hospitals, doctors, nursing homes, pharmacies, and other medical providers that transmit health information.
cards.explanation: Hospitals, doctors, nursing homes, pharmacies, and other medical providers.

cards.question: Official definition: “healthcare clearinghouses”
cards.answer: Healthcare clearinghouses: This includes public and private organizations, like billing services, that process or facilitate the processing of nonstandard health information and convert it into standard data types.
cards.explanation: A clearinghouse is a go-between. It changes health data into a standard format.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”. The manual adds that a clearinghouse is usually the go-between for a provider and a payer.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “healthcare clearinghouses” from memory.
cards.answer: Healthcare clearinghouses: This includes public and private organizations, like billing services, that process or facilitate the processing of nonstandard health information and convert it into standard data types.
cards.explanation: Three parts: public and private organizations like billing services, they process nonstandard health information, and they convert it into standard data types.

cards.question: Official definition: the “HIPAA Privacy Rule”
cards.answer: The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the use and disclosure of individuals' health information, referred to as protected health information.
cards.explanation: The Privacy Rule says who may use or show health information.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”. The rule took effect in 2003.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “HIPAA Privacy Rule”?
options: The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the use and disclosure of individuals' health information, referred to as protected health information.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes maximum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the use and disclosure of individuals' health information, referred to as protected health information.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the storage and backup of individuals' health information, referred to as protected health information.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the use and disclosure of individuals' financial information, referred to as protected financial information.
options_why: It says maximum. The real word is minimum.
It says storage and backup. The real words are use and disclosure.
It says financial. The rule is about health information.
cards.answer: The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the use and disclosure of individuals' health information, referred to as protected health information.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: minimum standards, patient's privacy, use and disclosure, and protected health information.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “HIPAA Privacy Rule” from memory.
cards.answer: The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting a patient's privacy and regulates the use and disclosure of individuals' health information, referred to as protected health information.
cards.explanation: Three parts: minimum standards, protecting the privacy of the patient, and the name of the data (protected health information).

cards.question: Official definition: the “HIPAA Security Rule”
cards.answer: The HIPAA Security Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting PHI that is stored or transferred in electronic form.
cards.explanation: The Security Rule is about the same health data, but when it is on a computer or on a network.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”. The rule took effect in 2003. It puts the Privacy Rule into practice with technical, physical, and administrative controls.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “HIPAA Security Rule”?
options: The HIPAA Security Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting PHI that is stored or transferred in paper form.
The HIPAA Security Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting PHI that is only stored in electronic form.
The HIPAA Security Rule establishes maximum standards for protecting PII that is stored or transferred in electronic form.
The HIPAA Security Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting PHI that is stored or transferred in electronic form.
options_why: It says paper form. The Security Rule is about electronic form.
It leaves out data that is transferred, and it adds the word only.
It says maximum, and it says PII. The real words are minimum and PHI.
cards.answer: The HIPAA Security Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting PHI that is stored or transferred in electronic form.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: minimum standards, PHI, stored or transferred, and electronic form.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “HIPAA Security Rule” from memory.
cards.answer: The HIPAA Security Rule establishes minimum standards for protecting PHI that is stored or transferred in electronic form.
cards.explanation: Three parts: minimum standards, protecting PHI, and stored or transferred in electronic form.

cards.question: A hospital keeps patient files on a computer. Which HIPAA rule is mainly about protecting files in electronic form?
options: The Privacy Rule
The Security Rule
The Safeguards Rule
The Financial Privacy Rule
options_why: The Privacy Rule is about the use and disclosure of health information in general.
This is a rule of GLBA, the law for banks.
This is also a rule of GLBA, the law for banks.
cards.answer: The Security Rule
cards.explanation: The Security Rule sets the standards for PHI that is stored or sent in electronic form.

cards.question: Which of these is a healthcare provider?
options: A health insurance company
A billing service that puts data in a standard format
A hospital
A government program that pays for care
options_why: It pays for care, so it is a health plan.
It is a go-between, so it is a clearinghouse.
It pays for care, so it is a health plan.
cards.answer: A hospital
cards.explanation: Providers give care. Hospitals, doctors, nursing homes, and pharmacies are providers.

cards.question: A company changes hospital bills into a standard format and passes them to insurers. What is this company?
options: A healthcare clearinghouse
A healthcare provider
A health plan
A company that HIPAA does not cover
options_why: Providers give care. This company does not treat patients.
Plans pay for care. This company does not pay.
The manual names billing services as clearinghouses, and they are covered.
cards.answer: A healthcare clearinghouse
cards.explanation: A clearinghouse is the go-between that converts health data into standard data types.

cards.question: A pharmacy sends a customer's list of medicines to the customer's employer by mistake. Which HIPAA rule does this MOST clearly break?
options: The Security Rule, because a hard drive failed
No rule, because a pharmacy is not covered by HIPAA
The Privacy Rule, because PHI went to someone who should not see it
The Safeguards Rule, because the data is financial
options_why: No hard drive failed here. The data went to the wrong person.
A pharmacy is a healthcare provider, so it is covered.
This is a GLBA rule, and this data is health data.
cards.answer: The Privacy Rule, because PHI went to someone who should not see it
cards.explanation: The Privacy Rule controls the use and disclosure of PHI. Showing it to an employer is not allowed.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a covered entity under HIPAA?
options: A health insurance company
A company that sells shoes online
A hospital
A billing service for health data
options_why: It is a health plan, so it is covered.
It is a healthcare provider, so it is covered.
It is a healthcare clearinghouse, so it is covered.
cards.answer: A company that sells shoes online
cards.explanation: The three groups are health plans, healthcare providers, and healthcare clearinghouses.

cards.question: A clinic stores patient records on a server. Which action is BEST to follow the Security Rule?
options: Use only a strong password on the server
Use only a locked door to the server room
Train the staff and use no technical controls
Use technical, physical, and administrative controls together
options_why: One control is not enough. The rule asks for three kinds of controls.
A door is a physical control. Technical and administrative controls are also needed.
Training is an administrative control. The rule also needs technical controls.
cards.answer: Use technical, physical, and administrative controls together
cards.explanation: The Security Rule puts the Privacy Rule into practice with technical, physical, and administrative controls.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”.

cards.question: A new clinic opens. The manager asks if HIPAA covers it. What should she check FIRST?
options: If the clinic has more than 100 patients
If the clinic is a health plan, a provider, or a clearinghouse
If the clinic keeps its files on computers
If the patients live in the same state
options_why: HIPAA covers organizations by their type, not by their size.
The rules matter for both, but the first question is the type of organization.
Where the patients live is not the test.
cards.answer: If the clinic is a health plan, a provider, or a clearinghouse
cards.explanation: HIPAA applies to covered entities. So the first step is to find out if the clinic is one of the three types.

cards.question: For which purpose may PHI be used under HIPAA?
options: To send ads about new products to patients
To give to any company that asks for it
Only to give healthcare services and to bill for them
To share with the patient's employer whenever the employer asks
options_why: Advertising is not care or billing.
PHI must be protected against improper disclosure.
An employer is not part of care or billing.
cards.answer: Only to give healthcare services and to bill for them
cards.explanation: The manual says PHI may be used strictly to perform and bill for healthcare services.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996”.

cards.question: Which range of civil fines is set for a HIPAA violation?
options: From 100 to 50,000 dollars per violation
From 100 to 5,000 dollars per violation
From 1,000 to 100,000 dollars per violation
From 50,000 to 1.5 million dollars per violation
options_why: The top amount is 50,000 dollars, not 5,000.
The range starts at 100 dollars and stops at 50,000 dollars.
1.5 million dollars is the yearly maximum for similar violations.
cards.answer: From 100 to 50,000 dollars per violation
cards.explanation: Civil fines go from 100 to 50,000 dollars per violation, with a yearly maximum of 1.5 million dollars for similar violations.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on HIPAA.

cards.question: In what year did the HIPAA Privacy Rule and Security Rule take effect?
options: In 1996, the year when the law was signed
In 1999, the year of the GLBA law
In 2009, six years after the rules took effect
In 2003, seven years after the law was signed
options_why: The law was signed in 1996. The rules started later.
1999 is the year of the GLBA law.
2009 is a later year. The rules started in 2003.
cards.answer: In 2003, seven years after the law was signed
cards.explanation: HIPAA was signed in 1996. Its two rules each took effect in 2003.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on HIPAA.

cards.question: How are the Privacy Rule and the Security Rule related?
options: The Security Rule replaces the Privacy Rule
They protect different people, so they are not related
The Security Rule puts the Privacy Rule into practice with controls
The Privacy Rule is about passwords and the Security Rule is about laws
options_why: Both rules exist together. One does not replace the other.
Both protect the PHI of patients.
It is the other way around. Privacy is about use and disclosure, and Security is about controls.
cards.answer: The Security Rule puts the Privacy Rule into practice with controls
cards.explanation: The Privacy Rule says who can see PHI. The Security Rule gives the controls that make this happen.

cards.question: When was HIPAA signed, and when did its two rules take effect?
cards.answer: The law was signed in 1996. The Privacy Rule and the Security Rule took effect in 2003.
cards.explanation: Seven years between the law and its rules: 1996, then 2003.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on HIPAA.

cards.question: What is PHI?
cards.answer: Protected health information. It is the health data of a person that HIPAA protects.
cards.explanation: Think of the doctor's file: illness, medicines, test results.

cards.question: What is a covered entity?
cards.answer: An organization that must follow HIPAA. It is a health plan, a healthcare provider, or a healthcare clearinghouse.
cards.explanation: Think: who pays, who treats, and who converts the data.

cards.question: What civil fines can a HIPAA violation bring?
cards.answer: From 100 to 50,000 dollars per violation. The maximum is 1.5 million dollars per year for similar violations.
cards.explanation: Two numbers: 50,000 dollars per violation and 1.5 million dollars per year.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on HIPAA.

cards.question: What criminal penalties can HIPAA bring?
cards.answer: Fines up to 250,000 dollars, and up to 10 years in prison.
cards.explanation: Criminal means that the person can go to court, not only pay a civil fine.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on HIPAA.

concepts.name: The HITECH Act: making HIPAA stronger

paragraphes: In the past, your medical file was on paper, in a binder. Today, it is on a computer.
This is handy for doctors. But if a digital file leaks, thousands of people can be hurt at once.
In 2009, the United States passed the HITECH Act. It pushes digital health files. It also makes the protection stronger.

decouverte.comme: When there are more cars on the road, the police add more speed cameras and raise the fines.
decouverte.enVrai: More electronic health records (EHR) means more risk. So the HITECH Act added tougher penalties for people who break HIPAA. The image stops here. A speed camera punishes after the event. HITECH also forces you to warn the people hurt by a leak.

decouverte.question: HITECH pushes digital health files. What does the law worry about?
options: More risks for security and privacy
Fewer doctors available
More expensive computers
decouverte.answer: More risks for security and privacy
decouverte.explanation: More data online means more targets for hackers and more chances for mistakes. So the law made the protections stronger.

decouverte.texte: A clinic finds out that an unprotected (unsecured) file leaked. This kind of leak is called a breach. The clinic must warn the people affected within 60 days. If 500 people or more are affected, it must also warn the US health department and a major media outlet.

cards.question: Official definition: the “HITECH Act”
cards.answer: The Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act, referred to as the HITECH Act, was enacted under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009.
cards.explanation: HITECH was born in 2009, inside a big law about the economy.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “HITECH Act” from memory.
cards.answer: The Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act, referred to as the HITECH Act, was enacted under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the full name, the short name HITECH Act, and the 2009 law that carried it.

cards.question: Official definition: what HITECH changes for HIPAA
cards.answer: As such, the HITECH Act extended HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing tougher penalties for HIPAA compliance violations.
cards.explanation: HITECH does not replace HIPAA. It makes HIPAA stronger with tougher penalties.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009”. The manual says that the highest penalties went up to 1.5 million dollars per violation category, per year.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of what HITECH changes for HIPAA?
options: As such, the HITECH Act extended HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing tougher penalties for HIPAA compliance violations.
As such, the HITECH Act extended HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing lighter penalties for HIPAA compliance violations.
As such, the HITECH Act replaced HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing tougher penalties for HIPAA compliance violations.
As such, the HITECH Act extended HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing tougher penalties for HIPAA training violations.
options_why: It says lighter. The real word is tougher.
It says replaced. The real word is extended.
It says training violations. The real words are compliance violations.
cards.answer: As such, the HITECH Act extended HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing tougher penalties for HIPAA compliance violations.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: extended HIPAA privacy protections, and imposing tougher penalties.

cards.question: Say the official definition of what HITECH changes for HIPAA from memory.
cards.answer: As such, the HITECH Act extended HIPAA privacy protections by improving security and privacy protections for healthcare data by imposing tougher penalties for HIPAA compliance violations.
cards.explanation: Three steps: extend HIPAA, improve the protections, and impose tougher penalties.

cards.question: Official definition: the HIPAA “Breach Notification Rule”
cards.answer: Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of unsecured protected health information to affected parties within 60 days of discovery of the breach.
cards.explanation: If unprotected health data leaks, you must warn the people affected within 60 days.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009”. This rule was added by HITECH.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the HIPAA “Breach Notification Rule”?
options: Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of unsecured protected health information to affected parties within 30 days of discovery of the breach.
Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of unsecured protected health information to affected parties within 60 days of the start of the breach.
Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of any protected health information to the media within 60 days of discovery of the breach.
Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of unsecured protected health information to affected parties within 60 days of discovery of the breach.
options_why: It says 30 days. The real number is 60 days.
The 60 days count from the discovery of the breach, not from its start.
It says the media and any data. The real sentence says affected parties and unsecured data.
cards.answer: Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of unsecured protected health information to affected parties within 60 days of discovery of the breach.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: covered entities, disclose a breach, unsecured, affected parties, and 60 days of discovery.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the HIPAA “Breach Notification Rule” from memory.
cards.answer: Under this rule, covered entities are required to disclose a breach of unsecured protected health information to affected parties within 60 days of discovery of the breach.
cards.explanation: Who must act, what they must do, for which data, and the 60 days from discovery.

cards.question: Which law added the duty to warn people when unprotected health data leaks?
options: COPPA
The HITECH Act
The Privacy Act of 1974
GLBA
options_why: COPPA is about children under 13 online.
This law is about government agencies.
GLBA is about banks and similar companies.
cards.answer: The HITECH Act
cards.explanation: HITECH added the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule.

cards.question: What did the HITECH Act change about HIPAA?
options: It made protections stronger and penalties tougher
It replaced HIPAA with a new law about electronic files
It removed the Security Rule
It made HIPAA apply only to paper files
options_why: HITECH extended HIPAA. It did not replace it.
The Security Rule stayed in place.
HITECH was made to push electronic health records.
cards.answer: It made protections stronger and penalties tougher
cards.explanation: HITECH extended HIPAA privacy protections with tougher penalties for violations.

cards.question: Why did the HITECH Act expect more security and privacy risks?
options: It forbade electronic health records
It made paper files easier to steal from the hospitals
It promoted wider use of electronic health records
It ended the rules of the Security Rule
options_why: It did the opposite. It promoted them.
The law is about digital records, not paper.
The rules stayed. HITECH made them stronger.
cards.answer: It promoted wider use of electronic health records
cards.explanation: More electronic health records means more data online, so there are more risks.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the HITECH Act.

cards.question: A clinic finds that an unprotected patient file leaked. 300 patients are affected. Which action is BEST?
options: Warn the patients, the health department, and a major media outlet
Warn only the health department
Warn nobody, because fewer than 500 patients are affected
Warn the affected patients within 60 days of discovery
options_why: This extra step is for leaks that affect 500 people or more.
The affected people must be told too.
The duty to warn the affected people has no minimum number.
cards.answer: Warn the affected patients within 60 days of discovery
cards.explanation: The affected people must always be warned within 60 days of discovery. The 500 limit adds more parties to warn.

cards.question: A clinic loses an unprotected file of 800 patients. Which answer MOST completely describes who it must warn?
options: The patients only
The patients, the US health department, and a major media outlet
The US health department only
The patients and the local police
options_why: With 500 people or more, other parties must be warned too.
The affected patients must also be told.
The police are not named in the rule.
cards.answer: The patients, the US health department, and a major media outlet
cards.explanation: With 500 people or more, the clinic also warns the US health department (HHS) and a major media outlet.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the HITECH Act.

cards.question: Which action is NOT required by the Breach Notification Rule?
options: Telling the people who are affected
Telling the US health department when 500 people or more are affected
Telling a major media outlet when 500 people or more are affected
Paying money to each person affected by the leak
options_why: The rule requires this within 60 days.
The rule requires this for large breaches.
The rule requires this for large breaches.
cards.answer: Paying money to each person affected by the leak
cards.explanation: The rule is about warning people and authorities. It does not ask to pay the people affected.

cards.question: Which list puts these events in order, from the oldest to the newest?
options: The HITECH Act is passed, then HIPAA is signed, then its rules take effect
HIPAA is signed, the HITECH Act is passed, its rules take effect
HIPAA is signed, its rules take effect, the HITECH Act is passed
Its rules take effect, HIPAA is signed, the HITECH Act is passed
options_why: HITECH came last, in 2009.
The rules took effect in 2003, before HITECH in 2009.
The law must be signed before its rules take effect.
cards.answer: HIPAA is signed, its rules take effect, the HITECH Act is passed
cards.explanation: HIPAA was signed in 1996. Its rules took effect in 2003. HITECH came in 2009.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1.

cards.question: What is the highest yearly penalty that HITECH set for each violation category?
options: 1.5 million dollars
250,000 dollars per year
50,000 dollars
100,000 dollars
options_why: This is the highest criminal fine of HIPAA.
This is the highest civil fine of HIPAA for one violation.
This is a civil fine of GLBA for an organization.
cards.answer: 1.5 million dollars
cards.explanation: Under HITECH, the maximum financial penalties went up to 1.5 million dollars per violation category, per year.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the HITECH Act.

cards.question: A leak of unsecured PHI is found. From which moment do the 60 days to warn people start?
options: From the day the leak began
From the day the leak is discovered
From the day the patients complain
From the day the health department asks
options_why: The clock starts at discovery, not at the start.
The clinic must not wait for complaints.
The duty exists without any request.
cards.answer: From the day the leak is discovered
cards.explanation: The rule says within 60 days of discovery of the breach.

cards.question: A hospital moves all patient files from paper to a computer system. Which action is BEST, in the spirit of HITECH?
options: Keep the same protections as for paper
Cut the protections, because computers are safe
Skip the Privacy Rule, because the software handles it
Add stronger protections, because digital files bring more risks
options_why: Digital files can leak in large numbers, so they need more protection.
Computers are not safe by themselves. HITECH expects more risks.
Software does not replace the rules that cover PHI.
cards.answer: Add stronger protections, because digital files bring more risks
cards.explanation: HITECH expected more risks from electronic records, so it made the protections stronger.

cards.question: In which year was HITECH passed, and inside which larger law?
cards.answer: In 2009, under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act.
cards.explanation: 2009: a big law about the economy, with a part about digital health.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the HITECH Act.

cards.question: What is the deadline to warn the people affected by a breach?
cards.answer: Within 60 days of the discovery of the breach.
cards.explanation: The clock starts the day the leak is found, not the day it happened.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the HITECH Act.

cards.question: From how many affected people must the health department and a media outlet also be warned?
cards.answer: From 500 people or more.
cards.explanation: A small leak concerns the people affected. A big leak is also made public.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The department is the US Department of Health and Human Services.

cards.question: What does the HITECH Act promote?
cards.answer: The wider use of electronic health records (EHRs).
cards.explanation: Digital records are handy, but they bring more risks.

cards.question: What is the highest financial penalty that HITECH set?
cards.answer: 1.5 million dollars per violation category, per year.
cards.explanation: The limit is yearly, and it is separate for each category of violation.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the HITECH Act.

concepts.name: The European road to the GDPR

paragraphes: An American company gets data from its customers in Europe. Europe protects this data more strictly than the United States.
If the rules are different, which side is right? For years, both sides looked for a deal.
This planet tells the story of the first European texts and two deals with the United States. A later law, the GDPR, replaced these texts.

decouverte.comme: If each class had its own rules, students would be lost. One shared rulebook avoids this.
decouverte.enVrai: Before 1995, each European country had its own rules. In 1995, a directive set shared principles. A directive is a text that tells each country what to achieve. Each country then wrote its own law.

decouverte.question: A deal between Europe and the United States was judged invalid in 2015. A new deal was made in 2016. What happened to the new deal in 2020?
options: It was also declared invalid
It became a European law
The two sides stopped exchanging data
decouverte.explanation: The same court canceled both deals. Guessing is fine here. You will learn the dates on this planet.

decouverte.texte: With Safe Harbor, a US company could say by itself that it followed the privacy rules. It is like a student who gives their own grade. In 2015, a European court judged this deal invalid.

cards.question: Official definition: the “Data Protection Directive”
cards.answer: The Data Protection Directive, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Parliament in 1995.
cards.explanation: The first big European text about personal data. It dates from 1995.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Data Protection Directive (EU)”. The manual says that the GDPR replaced it later.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “Data Protection Directive”?
options: The Data Protection Directive, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Parliament in 1995.
The Data Protection Directive, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Commission in 1995.
The Data Protection Directive, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Parliament in 1998.
The Data Protection Act, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Parliament in 1995.
options_why: It names the European Commission. The manual says the European Parliament.
The year is 1995. The year 1998 is for the UK Data Protection Act.
The Data Protection Act is the UK law. The European text is the Data Protection Directive.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Directive, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Parliament in 1995.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: Data Protection Directive, Directive 95/46/EC, European Parliament, and 1995.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “Data Protection Directive” from memory.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Directive, officially known as Directive 95/46/EC, was enacted by the European Parliament in 1995.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the name, the official number, and the institution that passed it.

cards.question: Official definition: the British “Data Protection Act”
cards.answer: The Data Protection Act was established by the United Kingdom Parliament to enact the provisions within the EU's Data Protection Directive.
cards.explanation: It is the British version of the European directive.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Data Protection Act 1998 (UK)”. The 1998 act was replaced by the Data Protection Act 2018, which supports the GDPR.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the British “Data Protection Act” from memory.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Act was established by the United Kingdom Parliament to enact the provisions within the EU's Data Protection Directive.
cards.explanation: Three parts: who established it (the UK Parliament), what it does (enact the provisions), and the European text it applies.

cards.question: Official definition: “Safe Harbor”
cards.answer: The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is an agreement between the United States and European Union, established between 1998 and 2000, that was developed to reconcile differences between U.S. and EU privacy laws.
cards.explanation: Safe Harbor was a bridge between two different sets of laws, in the US and in the EU.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Safe Harbor”. The manual adds that a US company could self-certify, and that a European court judged the deal invalid in 2015.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “Safe Harbor”?
options: The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is an agreement between the United States and European Union, established between 2015 and 2016, that was developed to reconcile differences between U.S. and EU privacy laws.

The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is an agreement between the United States and European Union, established between 1998 and 2000, that was developed to reconcile differences between U.S. and EU privacy laws.

The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is a law of the European Union, established between 1998 and 2000, that was developed to reconcile differences between U.S. and EU privacy laws.

The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is an agreement between the United States and European Union, established between 1998 and 2000, that was developed to replace U.S. and EU privacy laws.
options_why: The dates are wrong. Safe Harbor was established between 1998 and 2000.
It says a law of the EU. Safe Harbor was an agreement between two sides.
It says replace. The aim was to reconcile the differences, not to replace the laws.
cards.answer: The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is an agreement between the United States and European Union, established between 1998 and 2000, that was developed to reconcile differences between U.S. and EU privacy laws.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: an agreement between the United States and European Union, 1998 and 2000, and reconcile differences.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “Safe Harbor” from memory.
cards.answer: The International Safe Harbor Privacy Principles, often short-handed as just "Safe Harbor," is an agreement between the United States and European Union, established between 1998 and 2000, that was developed to reconcile differences between U.S. and EU privacy laws.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the full name, an agreement between the US and the EU, and its goal: to reconcile differences between the laws.

cards.question: Official definition: the “EU-US Privacy Shield”
cards.answer: The EU-US Privacy Shield was the second attempt by the European Union and United States to agree upon principles to mutually regulate the exchange of personal data between the two jurisdictions.
cards.explanation: The Privacy Shield was the second try at a deal, after Safe Harbor.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “EU-US Privacy Shield”. It was reached in 2016 and declared invalid by the same court by 2020.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “EU-US Privacy Shield” from memory.
cards.answer: The EU-US Privacy Shield was the second attempt by the European Union and United States to agree upon principles to mutually regulate the exchange of personal data between the two jurisdictions.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the name, the rank (second attempt), and the goal: agree on principles for exchanging personal data.

cards.question: Which text is the first big privacy law of the European Union?
options: The GDPR
The EU-US Privacy Shield
The Data Protection Directive of 1995
The Safe Harbor principles
options_why: The GDPR came later and replaced the directive.
This is a deal with the United States, not a European law.
This is also a deal with the United States.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Directive of 1995
cards.explanation: The Data Protection Directive was the first major privacy law in the European Union.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Data Protection Directive (EU)”.

cards.question: What was Safe Harbor?
options: A deal between the US and the EU about privacy
A European privacy law that applies only in the United Kingdom
A US law about children online
A European court that judged privacy cases
options_why: The UK law is the Data Protection Act. Safe Harbor was a deal.
The US law about children online is COPPA.
The court is the European Court of Justice, which judged Safe Harbor invalid.
cards.answer: A deal between the US and the EU about privacy
cards.explanation: Safe Harbor was made to reconcile the differences between US and EU privacy laws.

cards.question: What did the UK Data Protection Act 1998 do?
options: It created the Safe Harbor deal
It put the rules of the EU directive into UK law
It ended the Data Protection Directive
It replaced the GDPR in the UK
options_why: Safe Harbor was a deal between the US and the EU.
It applied the directive in the UK. It did not end it.
The GDPR came later. The 1998 act was older.
cards.answer: It put the rules of the EU directive into UK law
cards.explanation: The act was established by the UK Parliament to enact the provisions of the EU directive.

cards.question: In 2018, a European company wants to send personal data to a US partner. Which deal could MOST likely cover this?
options: Safe Harbor
The Data Protection Directive
The Data Protection Act 1998
The EU-US Privacy Shield
options_why: It was judged invalid in 2015, before 2018.
It is a European text, not a deal with the United States.
It is a UK law, not a deal with the United States.
cards.answer: The EU-US Privacy Shield
cards.explanation: The Privacy Shield was reached in 2016 and declared invalid by 2020. So it was valid in 2018.

cards.question: Which of these events came FIRST?
options: Safe Harbor was judged invalid
The Privacy Shield was reached
The Data Protection Directive was passed
The Privacy Shield was declared invalid
options_why: This happened in 2015.
This happened in 2016.
This happened by 2020.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Directive was passed
cards.explanation: The directive is from 1995. It came before all the other events.

cards.question: What happened to Safe Harbor in 2015?
options: The European Court of Justice ruled that it was invalid
It became a European law that all member countries must follow
The GDPR replaced it
The US Congress ended it
options_why: It stayed a deal and was ruled invalid.
The GDPR was established in 2016 and replaced the 1995 directive.
A European court ended it, not the US Congress.
cards.answer: The European Court of Justice ruled that it was invalid
cards.explanation: After 2015, the Privacy Shield replaced Safe Harbor.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Safe Harbor”.

cards.question: Which statement about the EU-US Privacy Shield is NOT true?
options: It was the second attempt to agree on principles
It was reached in 2016
It was the first attempt at a deal, before Safe Harbor
The same court that judged Safe Harbor declared it invalid
options_why: This is true. Safe Harbor was the first attempt.
This is true. It came less than a year after Safe Harbor was ruled invalid.
This is true. The European Court of Justice did it by 2020.
cards.answer: It was the first attempt at a deal, before Safe Harbor
cards.explanation: The Privacy Shield was the second attempt. Safe Harbor was the first.

cards.question: A US company in 1999 wants to say by itself that it follows the agreed privacy rules. Which deal BEST fits this case?
options: The EU-US Privacy Shield
Safe Harbor
The GDPR
The UK Data Protection Act
options_why: It was reached in 2016, long after 1999.
The GDPR is a law, and it was established in 2016.
This is a UK law, not a deal with the United States.
cards.answer: Safe Harbor
cards.explanation: Under Safe Harbor, a US company could self-certify that it met the privacy requirements.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Safe Harbor”.

cards.question: Why were deals like Safe Harbor needed?
options: The EU had no privacy rules at all
Companies wanted to avoid all privacy laws
The GDPR asked for them in 1998
The privacy laws of the US and the EU are different
options_why: The EU had the directive of 1995.
The deals were made to reconcile the laws, not to avoid them.
The GDPR came later, in 2016.
cards.answer: The privacy laws of the US and the EU are different
cards.explanation: A deal helps personal data to move between two sides that have different rules.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: Safe Harbor was developed to reconcile differences between US and EU privacy laws.

cards.question: Which text is the British version of the European directive?
options: The Data Protection Act 1998
The Data Protection Act 2018, passed later
The Safe Harbor principles
The EU-US Privacy Shield
options_why: It came later and supports the GDPR.
This is a deal between the US and the EU.
This is also a deal between the US and the EU.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Act 1998
cards.explanation: The 1998 act was written to apply the directive in the United Kingdom.

cards.question: In which year was the European data protection directive passed?
cards.answer: In 1995 (Directive 95/46/EC), by the European Parliament.
cards.explanation: The number 95 in 95/46/EC helps you to remember the year.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Data Protection Directive (EU)”.

cards.question: When was Safe Harbor judged invalid, and by whom?
cards.answer: In 2015, by the European Court of Justice.
cards.explanation: The Privacy Shield replaced it soon after.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Safe Harbor”.

cards.question: When was the Privacy Shield reached, and when was it declared invalid?
cards.answer: It was reached in 2016. It was declared invalid by 2020, by the same court.
cards.explanation: A short deal: about four years.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “EU-US Privacy Shield”.

cards.question: Which text replaced the UK Data Protection Act 1998?
cards.answer: The Data Protection Act 2018, which supports the GDPR.
cards.explanation: Same name, two eras: 1998 for the directive, 2018 for the GDPR.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Data Protection Act 1998 (UK)”.

cards.question: What could a US company do under Safe Harbor?
cards.answer: It could self-certify. It said by itself that it met the agreed privacy rules.
cards.explanation: Think of a student who gives their own grade.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Safe Harbor”.

concepts.name: The GDPR: scope, rights and roles

decouverte.titre: A site that asks your permission
paragraphes: You visit a clothing site. It asks your permission to use your data. You can also ask it to erase your data.
This is not by chance. A European law makes companies respect you, even if the company is on the other side of the world.
This law is the GDPR, short for General Data Protection Regulation. The official manual says most people see it as the strongest data privacy law in the world.

decouverte.titre: A life jacket that follows you
decouverte.comme: Your life jacket protects you on any lake. The protection follows you everywhere.
decouverte.enVrai: The GDPR protects the data of people in the European Union (EU), wherever the company is. The image stops here. You wear the jacket yourself. The law makes the company act.
