decouverte.question: A company in Canada keeps the data of customers who live in France. Does the GDPR apply to it?
options: No, it is outside Europe
Yes, because it handles data of people in the EU
Only if it has an office in Europe
decouverte.answer: Yes, because it handles data of people in the EU
decouverte.explanation: What matters is who the people are, not where the company is. An office in Europe is not needed.

decouverte.texte: Julie had an account on a game site. She does not play any more. She wants her data erased. Article 17 of the GDPR gives her this right in several situations. It is called the right to be forgotten, or the right to erasure.

decouverte.comme: A school cafeteria keeps the list of students' allergies. The cafeteria decides how to use the list. An IT company stores the list for the cafeteria. The students are the people on the list.
decouverte.enVrai: The data subject is the person whose data is used. The data controller keeps the data and decides how to use it. The data processor handles the data for the controller.

decouverte.texte: Article 25 asks you to think about privacy from the design stage of a product, and by default. This is called data protection by design and by default. Article 33 asks you to warn the authorities within 72 hours after you learn of a leak of personal data.

cards.question: Official definition: the “GDPR”
cards.answer: The GDPR is considered by most to be the world's strongest data privacy law.
cards.explanation: The GDPR is the world's top reference for data protection, according to the manual.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. The GDPR was established in 2016 and replaced the 1995 directive.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “GDPR” from memory.
cards.answer: The GDPR is considered by most to be the world's strongest data privacy law.
cards.explanation: Three parts: considered by most, the world's strongest, and data privacy law.

cards.question: Official definition: who the GDPR applies to
cards.answer: If your organization stores or processes the personal data of EU citizens or residents, then GDPR applies to you, whether or not your company is located in the EU.
cards.explanation: What counts is whose data it is, not where the company is.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This sentence is in a note of the GDPR section.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of who the GDPR applies to?
options: If your organization stores or processes the personal data of EU citizens or residents, then GDPR applies to you, only if your company is located in the EU.
If your organization stores or processes the personal data of EU citizens or residents, then GDPR applies to you, whether or not your company is located in the EU.
If your organization stores or processes the personal data of EU banks or governments, then GDPR applies to you, whether or not your company is located in the EU.
If your organization only processes the personal data of EU citizens or residents, then GDPR applies to you, whether or not your company is located in the EU.
options_why: It adds a condition about the place of the company. The real sentence says whether or not it is in the EU.
The GDPR protects the data of people, citizens or residents, not banks or governments.
It says only processes. The real sentence says stores or processes.
cards.answer: If your organization stores or processes the personal data of EU citizens or residents, then GDPR applies to you, whether or not your company is located in the EU.
cards.explanation: Key words: stores or processes, EU citizens or residents, and whether or not your company is in the EU.

cards.question: Say the official definition of who the GDPR applies to from memory.
cards.answer: If your organization stores or processes the personal data of EU citizens or residents, then GDPR applies to you, whether or not your company is located in the EU.
cards.explanation: Three parts: you store or process the data, of EU citizens or residents, wherever your company is.

cards.question: Official definition: Article 17 of the GDPR
cards.answer: Article 17 within the GDPR establishes a person's "right to be forgotten."
cards.explanation: Article 17 is the right to be forgotten. A person can ask to have their data erased.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This sentence is in a tip box of the GDPR section.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of Article 17 of the GDPR?
options: Article 33 within the GDPR establishes a person's "right to be forgotten."
Article 17 within the GDPR establishes a company's "right to be forgotten."
Article 17 within the GDPR establishes a person's "right to be forgotten."
Article 17 within the GDPR establishes a person's "right to be informed."
options_why: Article 33 is about warning the authorities within 72 hours.
It is the right of a person, not of a company.
The real right is to be forgotten, not to be informed.
cards.answer: Article 17 within the GDPR establishes a person's "right to be forgotten."
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: Article 17, a person's, and right to be forgotten.

cards.question: Say the official definition of Article 17 of the GDPR from memory.
cards.answer: Article 17 within the GDPR establishes a person's "right to be forgotten."
cards.explanation: The article number, whose right it is (a person's), and the name of the right.

cards.question: Official definition: the “data subject” and the right to erasure
cards.answer: This provision grants the data subject (i.e., the person whose data is being used) the right to have their personal data deleted if one of several circumstances exists and is a critical concept that information security professionals must consider when developing their data storage and retention policies.
cards.explanation: The data subject is the person whose data is used. This person can ask for the data to be deleted.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. The words “this provision” mean Article 17.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “data subject” and the right to erasure from memory.
cards.answer: This provision grants the data subject (i.e., the person whose data is being used) the right to have their personal data deleted if one of several circumstances exists and is a critical concept that information security professionals must consider when developing their data storage and retention policies.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the data subject, the right to have personal data deleted, and the link with data storage and retention policies.

cards.question: Official definition: GDPR Chapter 4 and the “data processors”
cards.answer: GDPR Chapter 4 contains several articles that establish requirements related to the data controller and processor and requires that data processors (i.e., an organization that stores and processes PII on behalf of a data controller) prioritize security and privacy.
cards.explanation: The processor works for the controller, but it must also protect the data.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. The manual says that Article 25 asks for data protection by design and by default.

cards.question: Say the official definition of GDPR Chapter 4 and the “data processors” from memory.
cards.answer: GDPR Chapter 4 contains several articles that establish requirements related to the data controller and processor and requires that data processors (i.e., an organization that stores and processes PII on behalf of a data controller) prioritize security and privacy.
cards.explanation: Remember the key phrase: on behalf of a data controller. The processor must prioritize security and privacy.

cards.question: A shop in Canada keeps data of customers who live in France. Does the GDPR apply to the shop?
options: No, because the shop is outside the EU
Only if the shop has an office in Europe
Only if the shop is very large
Yes, because it handles data of people in the EU
options_why: The place of the company does not decide. The people concerned do.
The manual does not ask for any office in Europe.
The manual does not limit the GDPR to large companies.
cards.answer: Yes, because it handles data of people in the EU
cards.explanation: As soon as an organization stores or processes data of EU citizens or residents, the GDPR applies.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note in the GDPR section.

cards.question: Who is the data subject in the GDPR?
options: The person whose data is used
The company that stores the data
The company that handles the data for another company
The office that sets the fines
options_why: This is the data controller.
This is the data processor.
This is a supervisory authority.
cards.answer: The person whose data is used
cards.explanation: The data subject is the person that the data is about.

cards.question: Which GDPR article gives a person the right to be forgotten?
options: Article 5
Article 17
Article 25
Article 33
options_why: Article 5 lists seven principles for processing personal data.
Article 25 is about data protection by design and by default.
Article 33 is about warning the authorities within 72 hours.
cards.answer: Article 17
cards.explanation: Article 17 lets a person have their data deleted in several situations.

cards.question: A cloud company stores a shop's customer list for the shop. The shop decides how to use the list. Which description BEST fits the cloud company?
options: A data controller
A data subject
A supervisory authority
A data processor
options_why: The shop decides how to use the data, so the shop is the controller.
The data subjects are the customers on the list.
An authority checks the rules and sets fines. It does not store the list.
cards.answer: A data processor
cards.explanation: The processor handles the data on behalf of the controller.

cards.question: A company learns of a personal data breach. Under Article 33, what must it do FIRST?
options: Notify the proper authorities within 60 days
Delete the data of all the customers
Notify the proper authorities within 72 hours
Wait until customers complain
options_why: Sixty days is the deadline of the HIPAA rule. The GDPR says 72 hours.
Article 33 asks for a notification, not for deletion.
The company must act when it becomes aware, without waiting.
cards.answer: Notify the proper authorities within 72 hours
cards.explanation: Article 33 asks data controllers to notify the proper authorities within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on Article 33.

cards.question: Which organization MOST clearly has to follow the GDPR?
options: A Brazilian start-up that has only Brazilian customers
A Brazilian start-up that stores data of German customers
A US bank that has only US residents as customers, in 50 states
A school in Japan that has no European students
options_why: No EU data is handled, so the GDPR does not apply.
No EU data is handled here either.
No EU data is handled in this school.
cards.answer: A Brazilian start-up that stores data of German customers
cards.explanation: What counts is the data of EU citizens or residents, not the place of the company.

cards.question: Which statement about the scope of the GDPR is NOT correct?
options: It applies only to companies that are located in the EU
It applies if you store personal data of EU residents
It applies if you process personal data of EU citizens or residents
It protects people even if the company is far away
options_why: This is correct. Storing the data is enough.
This is correct. Processing the data is enough.
This is correct. The place of the company does not matter.
cards.answer: It applies only to companies that are located in the EU
cards.explanation: The GDPR applies whether or not the company is located in the EU.

cards.question: A team builds a new app and wants to follow Article 25. What is the BEST approach?
options: Add privacy features later, after the app is released to its users
Ask each user to choose all the privacy settings
Wait for an audit before thinking about privacy
Think about privacy from the start and set safe default settings
options_why: Article 25 asks for privacy by design, from the start.
By default, the app should already protect the data.
Waiting is reactive. Article 25 asks to prevent problems.
cards.answer: Think about privacy from the start and set safe default settings
cards.explanation: Article 25 asks for data protection by design and by default.
cards.explanation_more: The manual only names the rule. The detail about safe default settings is a simple explanation from outside the manual.

cards.question: Why must people who plan data retention think about the right to be forgotten?
options: Because the GDPR forbids all deletion of data
Because data must be kept forever, so that the authorities can check it
Because a company must be able to find and delete data when asked
Because the right applies only to very old data
options_why: The right to be forgotten asks for deletion in several situations.
The GDPR does not ask to keep all data forever.
The right does not depend on how old the data is.
cards.answer: Because a company must be able to find and delete data when asked
cards.explanation: You cannot delete what you cannot find. So deletion must be planned in the retention policy.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: it is a critical concept for data storage and retention policies.

cards.question: Which text did the GDPR replace?
options: The Safe Harbor principles
The EU-US Privacy Shield deal with the United States
The Data Protection Act 2018
The Data Protection Directive of 1995
options_why: This was a deal with the United States, not a European law.
This was also a deal with the United States.
This UK act was made to support the GDPR.
cards.answer: The Data Protection Directive of 1995
cards.explanation: The GDPR was established in 2016 and replaced the 1995 directive.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”.

cards.question: In which year was the GDPR established, and what did it replace?
cards.answer: In 2016. It replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive.
cards.explanation: Twenty-one years between the directive and the GDPR.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”.

cards.question: What does Article 25 of the GDPR ask for?
cards.answer: Data protection by design and by default.
cards.explanation: Think about privacy from the start, not at the end.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The manual says this puts into law what security professionals have long recommended.

cards.question: Within what time must you warn the authorities of a personal data breach (Article 33)?
cards.answer: Within 72 hours of becoming aware of it.
cards.explanation: 72 hours is three days. Speed matters.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on Article 33.

cards.question: What is a data processor, in simple words?
cards.answer: An organization that stores and processes PII on behalf of a data controller.
cards.explanation: It works for the controller, but it must also protect the data.

cards.question: What is the right to be forgotten?
cards.answer: The right of a person to have their personal data deleted in some situations. It is in Article 17.
cards.explanation: Think of Julie, who wants her old game account data erased.

paragraphes: Your class representative writes down everyone's phone number to plan a trip.
She must say what the numbers are for. She must write down only what she needs. She must keep the numbers correct. If not, classmates stop trusting her.
The GDPR asks the same of companies, in its Article 5. Article 5 has seven principles. A principle is a basic rule. Here are the first four.

decouverte.comme: The class representative says: “I will use your numbers only for the trip.” She does not ask for your addresses. She fixes a wrong number.
decouverte.enVrai: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: follow the law and say clearly how you will use the data. Purpose limitation: announce a specific goal. Data minimization: take only what you need. Accuracy: keep the data correct and up to date.

decouverte.question: A game site asks for your religion before you can play. Which principle does this request mostly ignore?
options: Data minimization
Accuracy
Purpose limitation
decouverte.explanation: Asking for more than needed goes against data minimization. Accuracy is about correct data. Purpose limitation is about the announced goal.

decouverte.texte: The library asks for your name and address to lend you books. It says this is to send a reminder to return them. If you move, it updates your address. It does not ask for your religion or your parents' jobs.

cards.question: Official definition: Article 5 of the GDPR
cards.answer: GDPR Article 5 establishes and describes seven principles for processing personal data:
cards.explanation: Article 5 has seven principles. Remember the number seven.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of Article 5 of the GDPR from memory.
cards.answer: GDPR Article 5 establishes and describes seven principles for processing personal data:
cards.explanation: Three parts: establishes and describes, seven principles, and processing personal data.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “lawfulness, fairness, and transparency”
cards.answer: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with applicable laws and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.
cards.explanation: Follow the law, be honest, and tell the customer clearly how the data will be used.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 1 of Article 5.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the principle “lawfulness, fairness, and transparency”?
options: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with company rules and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.
Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with applicable laws and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.
Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with applicable laws and fully inform the customer of how their data was collected.
Lawfulness, fairness, and security: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with applicable laws and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.
options_why: It says company rules. The real words are applicable laws.
The duty is to say how the data will be used, not how it was collected.
The third word is transparency, not security.
cards.answer: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with applicable laws and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: applicable laws, and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “lawfulness, fairness, and transparency” from memory.
cards.answer: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency: Obtain and process personal data in accordance with applicable laws and fully inform the customer of how their data will be used.
cards.explanation: Three parts: obtain and process the data, follow the applicable laws, and fully inform the customer.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “purpose limitation”
cards.answer: Purpose limitation: Identify "specific, explicit, and legitimate" purpose for data collection, and inform them of such purpose.
cards.explanation: Choose a clear and legitimate goal before you collect data. Tell people about it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 2 of Article 5.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the principle “purpose limitation”?
options: Purpose limitation: Identify "specific, explicit, and legitimate" purpose for data collection, and inform them of such purpose.
Purpose limitation: Identify "general, flexible, and legitimate" purpose for data collection, and inform them of such purpose.
Purpose limitation: Identify "specific, explicit, and legitimate" purpose for data collection, and keep them unaware of such purpose.
Purpose limitation: Identify "specific, explicit, and legitimate" purpose for data storage, and inform them of such purpose.
options_why: The real words are specific and explicit. A general purpose is too vague.
The company must inform people about the purpose, not hide it.
It says data storage. The real words are data collection.
cards.answer: Purpose limitation: Identify "specific, explicit, and legitimate" purpose for data collection, and inform them of such purpose.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: specific, explicit, and legitimate, data collection, and inform them.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “purpose limitation” from memory.
cards.answer: Purpose limitation: Identify "specific, explicit, and legitimate" purpose for data collection, and inform them of such purpose.
cards.explanation: Three adjectives for the purpose, the collection, and the duty to inform.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “data minimization”
cards.answer: Data minimization: Collect and process the minimum amount of data necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
cards.explanation: Take only the data that you really need to give the promised service.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 3 of Article 5.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the principle “data minimization”?
options: Data minimization: Collect and process the maximum amount of data possible to provide the agreed-upon services.
Data minimization: Collect and process the minimum amount of data necessary to provide the best possible services.
Data minimization: Collect and process the minimum amount of data necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
Data minimization: Collect and process the minimum amount of data necessary to improve the agreed-upon services.
options_why: It says maximum. The real word is minimum.
It says best possible services. The real words are agreed-upon services.
It says improve. The real word is provide.
cards.answer: Data minimization: Collect and process the minimum amount of data necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the minimum amount of data, necessary, and the agreed-upon services.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “data minimization” from memory.
cards.answer: Data minimization: Collect and process the minimum amount of data necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
cards.explanation: Three parts: collect and process, the minimum amount of data, and the agreed-upon services.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “accuracy”
cards.answer: Accuracy: Ensure that personal data remains "accurate and where necessary kept up-to-date."
cards.explanation: The data must be correct. Update it when it is needed.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 4 of Article 5.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “accuracy” from memory.
cards.answer: Accuracy: Ensure that personal data remains "accurate and where necessary kept up-to-date."
cards.explanation: Make sure that personal data stays accurate, and up to date where necessary.

cards.question: A club asks for twelve pieces of information when three are enough. Which principle is ignored?
options: Data minimization
Purpose limitation
Accuracy
Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
options_why: This principle is about the goal that was announced.
This principle is about correct data.
This principle is about the law and about informing the customer.
cards.answer: Data minimization
cards.explanation: The club takes more than needed. Data minimization says to collect only the minimum necessary.

cards.question: A company keeps an old address for a customer who moved years ago. Which principle is ignored?
options: Data minimization
Accuracy
Purpose limitation
Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
options_why: The problem is not the amount of data. It is that the data is wrong.
The problem is not the goal. It is that the data is out of date.
Nothing here says that the law or the information was a problem.
cards.answer: Accuracy
cards.explanation: Accuracy asks that personal data stays correct and, where necessary, up to date.

cards.question: How many principles does Article 5 of the GDPR have?
options: Four
Five
Eleven
Seven
options_why: Four is only the number of principles on this planet.
Article 5 has the number five, but it has seven principles.
Eleven is too many. Article 5 has seven principles.
cards.answer: Seven
cards.explanation: Article 5 has seven principles. You learn four now and three on the next planet.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”.

cards.question: A gym asks for your phone number to warn you about canceled classes. Later it uses the number to sell products, and it never said so. Which principle is MOST clearly ignored?
options: Accuracy
Data minimization
Purpose limitation
None, because the gym owns the numbers
options_why: Nothing says that the numbers are wrong.
A number to warn about classes is justified. The problem is the later use.
The numbers are personal data. The law controls how they are used.
cards.answer: Purpose limitation
cards.explanation: The number was collected for one goal and used for another goal that nobody announced.

cards.question: Which action does NOT respect data minimization?
options: A library asks only for a name and an address to lend books
A recipe app asks for your location every minute
A shop asks only for the delivery address to send an order
A newsletter asks only for an email address
options_why: These are needed to lend books, so it respects the principle.
This is needed to send the order, so it respects the principle.
This is needed to send the newsletter, so it respects the principle.
cards.answer: A recipe app asks for your location every minute
cards.explanation: A recipe does not need to know where you are every minute. This is more data than the service needs.

cards.question: A company wants to start collecting data for a new service. What should it do FIRST to respect purpose limitation?
options: Identify a specific, explicit, and legitimate purpose, and tell the customers
Collect everything and decide the purpose later
Write a vague purpose such as “to improve things”
Hire a team to encrypt the data
options_why: The purpose must come before the collection.
The purpose must be specific and explicit, not vague.
Encryption helps security, but the first step is to choose and announce the purpose.
cards.answer: Identify a specific, explicit, and legitimate purpose, and tell the customers
cards.explanation: Purpose limitation asks for a clear goal before collection, and a duty to inform people about it.

cards.question: A company processes personal data in a way that breaks the law and hides this from the customer. Which principle is MOST affected?
options: Data minimization
Accuracy
Purpose limitation
Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
options_why: The problem is not the amount of data.
The problem is not that the data is wrong.
The problem is not a twisted goal. It is breaking the law and hiding it.
cards.answer: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
cards.explanation: The principle asks to follow the applicable laws and to fully inform the customer.

cards.question: A clothing site opens customer accounts. Which list of requested data BEST respects data minimization?
options: Name, address, religion, and health data
Name, address, and the jobs of the customer's parents
Name, delivery address, and a way to contact the customer
Name, address, and all the photos on the customer's phone
options_why: Religion and health data are not needed to sell clothes.
The parents' jobs are not needed to deliver an order.
The photos have nothing to do with the order.
cards.answer: Name, delivery address, and a way to contact the customer
cards.explanation: Each piece of data must serve the promised service. Delivery needs a name, an address, and a contact.

cards.question: Why must a company announce its goal before it collects data?
options: So the person can decide knowing how the data will be used
So the company can change the goal later, when it has new ideas
So the company can collect more data
So the company does not need to follow the law
options_why: The goal should be specific, so it cannot change at will.
Announcing a goal does not give the right to collect more.
The goal does not replace the law.
cards.answer: So the person can decide knowing how the data will be used
cards.explanation: People can only accept or refuse what they know.

cards.question: A customer asks why a newsletter form wants her blood type. What is the BEST response from the company?
options: Explain that more data is always better for the company and for customers
Remove the question, because it is not needed for a newsletter
Keep the question, but do not give a reason
Keep the question and make it optional in small print
options_why: More data than needed goes against data minimization.
The company must be open about how it uses data.
The data is still not needed, and small print is not open.
cards.answer: Remove the question, because it is not needed for a newsletter
cards.explanation: The best fix is to stop asking for data that the service does not need.

cards.question: Which principle says to collect only what is needed?
cards.answer: Data minimization.
cards.explanation: Minimum means as little as possible to give the service.

cards.question: Which principle says to announce a specific, explicit, and legitimate goal?
cards.answer: Purpose limitation.
cards.explanation: Purpose means goal: a clear, announced, legitimate goal.

cards.question: What does the accuracy principle ask?
cards.answer: That personal data stays accurate and, where necessary, up to date.
cards.explanation: Wrong data can lead to wrong decisions about a person.

cards.question: What does “lawfulness, fairness, and transparency” mean, in simple words?
cards.answer: Follow the law, be honest, and tell the customer how the data will be used.
cards.explanation: It is the honesty principle.

cards.question: Give an example of data that a clothing site does not need.
cards.answer: Religion or health data. The site only needs what is necessary to deliver the order.
cards.explanation: Ask: does this data serve the promised service?

paragraphes: At the end of the year, the school keeps your report cards for a set time. Then it destroys them.
It stores them in a locked cabinet. And if someone checks, it can show how it protected them.
These three habits match the last three principles of the GDPR. Keep data for less time. Protect it well. Be able to prove it.

decouverte.titre: The yogurt and its expiry date
decouverte.comme: A yogurt has an expiry date. After that date, it goes in the trash. It is kept in the fridge. And the shop can prove that it kept the yogurt cold.
decouverte.enVrai: Storage limitation: keep data only as long as you need it. Integrity and confidentiality: protect it from unauthorized access and from loss. Accountability: the controller must be able to prove that it follows the principles. Following the rules is called compliance.

decouverte.question: A shop keeps a customer's data ten years after the last purchase, for no reason. Which principle is ignored?
options: Storage limitation
Accuracy
Data minimization
decouverte.explanation: The problem is the length of time. The data is kept longer than needed. Data minimization is about the amount that you collect.

decouverte.texte: A company wants to show that it protects data well. It gets a recognized certification, for example ISO 27001. This is a way to show accountability to its customers.

decouverte.comme: Before you post a class photo, you blur the faces. You still see the class, but nobody is recognized.
decouverte.enVrai: Data anonymization removes what lets you identify a person. The manual names it as a technique to protect the identity of customers when necessary.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “storage limitation”
cards.answer: Storage limitation: Personal data may be stored only long as necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
cards.explanation: Keep data only as long as the service needs it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 5 of Article 5. The manual writes “only long as”. Learn it as it is.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the principle “storage limitation”?
options: Storage limitation: Personal data may be stored only long as necessary to improve the agreed-upon services.
Storage limitation: Personal data may be stored for a long time to provide the agreed-upon services.
Storage limitation: Personal data may be shared only long as necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
Storage limitation: Personal data may be stored only long as necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
options_why: It says improve. The real word is provide.
It allows a long time. The real sentence says only as long as necessary.
It says shared. The real word is stored.
cards.answer: Storage limitation: Personal data may be stored only long as necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: stored, only long as necessary, and provide the agreed-upon services.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “storage limitation” from memory.
cards.answer: Storage limitation: Personal data may be stored only long as necessary to provide the agreed-upon services.
cards.explanation: Three parts: personal data, the necessary time, and the agreed-upon services.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “integrity and confidentiality”
cards.answer: Integrity and confidentiality: Ensure appropriate security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
cards.explanation: Protect personal data from intruders and from accidents.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 6 of Article 5.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the principle “integrity and confidentiality”?
options: Integrity and confidentiality: Ensure maximum security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
Integrity and availability: Ensure appropriate security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
Integrity and confidentiality: Ensure appropriate security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
Integrity and confidentiality: Ensure appropriate security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and intentional loss or destruction.
options_why: It says maximum. The real word is appropriate.
The principle is called integrity and confidentiality, not availability.
It says intentional. The real word is accidental.
cards.answer: Integrity and confidentiality: Ensure appropriate security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: appropriate security, unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “integrity and confidentiality” from memory.
cards.answer: Integrity and confidentiality: Ensure appropriate security of personal data, and provide protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
cards.explanation: Three parts: appropriate security, protection against unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.

cards.question: Official definition: the principle “accountability”
cards.answer: Accountability: The data controller (i.e., the party that stores and processes the personal data) must be able to demonstrate compliance with all of these principles.
cards.explanation: Following the rules is not enough. You must be able to prove it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This is principle 7 of Article 5. The manual adds that many customers look for certifications like ISO 27001 to see this accountability.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the principle “accountability”?
options: Accountability: The data controller (i.e., the party that stores and processes the personal data) must be able to demonstrate compliance with some of these principles.
Accountability: The data controller (i.e., the party that stores and processes the personal data) must be able to promise compliance with all of these principles.
Accountability: The data subject (i.e., the person whose data is used) must be able to demonstrate compliance with all of these principles.
Accountability: The data controller (i.e., the party that stores and processes the personal data) must be able to demonstrate compliance with all of these principles.
options_why: It says some. The real word is all.
It says promise. The real word is demonstrate.
The data controller must show compliance, not the data subject.
cards.answer: Accountability: The data controller (i.e., the party that stores and processes the personal data) must be able to demonstrate compliance with all of these principles.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the data controller, demonstrate compliance, and all of these principles.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the principle “accountability” from memory.
cards.answer: Accountability: The data controller (i.e., the party that stores and processes the personal data) must be able to demonstrate compliance with all of these principles.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the data controller, must be able to demonstrate compliance, and with all of these principles.

cards.question: Official definition: anonymization in the principle “integrity and confidentiality”
cards.answer: This includes implementing data anonymization techniques to protect your customers' identities, where necessary.
cards.explanation: To anonymize data is to remove what lets you recognize a person.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”. This sentence follows the principle “integrity and confidentiality”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of anonymization in the principle “integrity and confidentiality” from memory.
cards.answer: This includes implementing data anonymization techniques to protect your customers' identities, where necessary.
cards.explanation: Three parts: data anonymization techniques, to protect customers' identities, and where necessary.

cards.question: A shop keeps a customer's data ten years after the last purchase, for no reason. Which principle is ignored?
options: Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
Data minimization
Storage limitation
Accountability
options_why: This principle is about the law and about informing the customer.
This is about how much data you collect, not how long you keep it.
This is about proving that you follow the rules.
cards.answer: Storage limitation
cards.explanation: Personal data may be stored only as long as it is needed for the agreed services.

cards.question: A clinic leaves patient files on a computer with no password. Which principle is ignored?
options: Integrity and confidentiality
Storage limitation
Accountability
Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
options_why: Nothing here is about how long the data is kept.
This is about proving compliance. The problem here is the protection itself.
Nothing here is about the law or about informing the customer.
cards.answer: Integrity and confidentiality
cards.explanation: With no password, anyone can open the files. The appropriate security is missing.

cards.question: Who must be able to prove that the principles are followed?
options: The data subject
The data controller
Only the data processor
The supervisory authority
options_why: The data subject is the person that the data is about.
The manual puts this duty on the data controller.
The authority checks and sets fines. It does not have to prove the company's compliance.
cards.answer: The data controller
cards.explanation: The controller keeps the data and decides how to use it. So it must be able to demonstrate compliance.

cards.question: A company wants to show customers that it protects data well. Which action BEST supports its accountability?
options: Tell customers that the data is safe, with no proof
Keep the security reports secret from everyone
Ask customers to trust the company
Get a recognized certification, such as ISO 27001
options_why: Words without proof do not show accountability.
Accountability needs the company to show proof.
Trust alone is not proof.
cards.answer: Get a recognized certification, such as ISO 27001
cards.explanation: A certification is proof given by an outside party. It shows accountability.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: many customers look for certifications like ISO 27001 to see accountability.

cards.question: Which action does NOT help storage limitation?
options: Erasing a customer's data when the account is closed
Keeping all customer data forever, in case it is useful
Keeping data only while the service needs it
Setting a date to delete old data
options_why: This helps. The data is not needed any more.
This is exactly what the principle asks.
This helps. It keeps the storage time short.
cards.answer: Keeping all customer data forever, in case it is useful
cards.explanation: Keeping data forever is the opposite of storage limitation.

cards.question: A company stores customer files. Which choice BEST protects them from unauthorized access and accidental loss?
options: Encryption of the files, with no other control
Backups of all the files, with no other control
Encryption and limited access, plus backups
A clear privacy notice only
options_why: Encryption helps against access, but it does not protect against accidental loss.
Backups help against loss, but they do not stop unauthorized access.
A notice informs people. It does not protect the files.
cards.answer: Encryption and limited access, plus backups
cards.explanation: The principle asks for appropriate security against both unauthorized access and accidental loss or destruction.

cards.question: Which situation MOST clearly shows a lack of accountability?
options: A company follows the rules but cannot prove it
A company deletes data when it is no longer needed
A company encrypts all of its files
A company collects only the data that it needs
options_why: This respects storage limitation.
This respects the principle of integrity and confidentiality.
This respects data minimization.
cards.answer: A company follows the rules but cannot prove it
cards.explanation: Accountability means being able to show proof of compliance with all the principles.

cards.question: What does data anonymization do?
options: It encrypts data so that only the key owner can read it
It copies data to a second server for safety
It deletes all data after one year
It removes what lets people identify a person
options_why: This is encryption. Anonymization removes the link to a person.
This is a backup, not anonymization.
This is about storage limitation.
cards.answer: It removes what lets people identify a person
cards.explanation: The manual names anonymization as a technique to protect the identity of customers when necessary.

cards.question: A customer closes her account. What does storage limitation say about her data?
options: Keep it forever, as a record of everything the customer did
Keep it only as long as needed for the agreed services
Sell it to other companies
Move it to a backup that nobody checks
options_why: The principle asks to keep data for a limited time.
The data is not for sale. The principle limits its use.
The data would still be stored, and nobody would control it.
cards.answer: Keep it only as long as needed for the agreed services
cards.explanation: Once the services end, the reason to keep the data goes away.

cards.question: A company shows its customers an ISO 27001 certificate. Which principle does this support?
options: Accountability
Storage limitation
Accuracy
Data minimization
options_why: A certificate does not delete data.
A certificate does not make data correct.
A certificate does not reduce the amount of data.
cards.answer: Accountability
cards.explanation: A certificate is a way to demonstrate compliance, which is accountability.

cards.question: What does storage limitation ask?
cards.answer: Keep personal data only as long as necessary to provide the agreed services.
cards.explanation: The key word is time.

cards.question: Which two dangers does the principle “integrity and confidentiality” protect against?
cards.answer: Unauthorized access, and accidental loss or destruction.
cards.explanation: Think of an intruder and of an accident.

cards.question: What does accountability ask of the data controller?
cards.answer: To be able to demonstrate compliance with all of the principles.
cards.explanation: Following the rules is not enough. You must be able to prove it.

cards.question: Name one way to show accountability.
cards.answer: Get a recognized certification, such as ISO 27001.
cards.explanation: A certification is proof given by an outside party.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “General Data Protection Regulation (EU)”.

cards.question: What is data anonymization?
cards.answer: A technique that protects the identity of customers, when necessary, by removing what points to a person.
cards.explanation: Think of blurring the faces on a photo.

decouverte.titre: A fine that depends on size
paragraphes: A small shop and a very large company make the same mistake. A fine of 1,000 euros only scares the shop.
So the GDPR sets a maximum based on worldwide revenue. Revenue is the money that a company earns by selling its products.
Let us look at these amounts, and at how the amount of a fine is chosen.

decouverte.titre: The speeding ticket depends on the offense
decouverte.comme: Driving 5 km/h too fast or 50 km/h too fast does not cost the same. And if you say sorry and fix things, the judge is kinder.
decouverte.enVrai: The GDPR has two levels of fines. The lower level covers some duties. The upper level covers the basic principles, the rights of people, and data transfers. Ten criteria help to set the amount.

decouverte.question: What is the highest fine for the most serious GDPR offenses?
options: 20 million or 4% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
5 million or 3% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
50 million or 6% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
decouverte.answer: 20 million or 4% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
decouverte.explanation: Guessing is normal. You must learn these numbers by heart. Seeing them here helps you remember them later.

decouverte.texte: Two companies have a data leak. The first one had protections, warned the authorities right away, and cooperated. The second one ignored the alerts, hid the leak, and refused to answer. The second company will probably get a heavier fine.

cards.question: Official definition: GDPR fines
cards.answer: The GDPR imposes stiff fines on data controllers and processors for noncompliance.
cards.explanation: The fines target both roles: the data controller and the data processor.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “GDPR Fines”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of GDPR fines from memory.
cards.answer: The GDPR imposes stiff fines on data controllers and processors for noncompliance.
cards.explanation: Three parts: stiff fines, data controllers and processors, and noncompliance.

cards.question: Official definition: the criteria for setting the amount of a fine
cards.answer: The following 10 criteria are to be used to determine the amount of the fine on a noncompliant firm:
cards.explanation: There are ten criteria. Remember the number ten.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “GDPR Fines”. Fines are set by the supervisory authorities of each member state.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the criteria for setting the amount of a fine from memory.
cards.answer: The following 10 criteria are to be used to determine the amount of the fine on a noncompliant firm:
cards.explanation: Three parts: the number (10 criteria), their use (the amount of the fine), and the firm concerned (noncompliant).

cards.question: Who sets the amount of a GDPR fine?
options: One central court for the whole EU
The person who made the complaint
The supervisory authority of each member state
The auditors of the company
options_why: The manual says fines are administered by each member state's authority.
The data subject can complain, but does not set the fine.
The company's own auditors do not set fines on the company.
cards.answer: The supervisory authority of each member state
cards.explanation: Each EU country has its own supervisory authority that sets the fines.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “GDPR Fines”.

cards.question: Which pair describes the upper level of GDPR fines?
options: 20 million or 4% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
10 million or 2% of the worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
20 million or 2% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
10 million or 4% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
options_why: This is the lower level.
The fixed amount is right, but the percentage of the upper level is 4%.
The percentage is right, but the fixed amount of the upper level is 20 million.
cards.answer: 20 million or 4% of worldwide revenue, whichever is higher
cards.explanation: Upper level: 20 million or 4%. Lower level: 10 million or 2%.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “GDPR Fines”. The manual does not name the currency. It is euros (outside the manual).

cards.question: What does “whichever is higher” mean for a GDPR fine?
options: Use the smaller of the two amounts that you calculate
Compare both amounts and use the bigger one
Use the fixed amount only
Use the percentage only
options_why: The rule uses the higher amount, not the lower one.
The percentage can be higher for a large company.
The fixed amount can be higher for a small company.
cards.answer: Compare both amounts and use the bigger one
cards.explanation: You calculate both amounts. Then you keep the larger one.

cards.question: A company has a worldwide revenue of 1 billion. It ignores a customer's right to erasure. What is the MOST that it can be fined?
options: 20 million
10 million
2 million
40 million
options_why: This is the fixed amount. But 4% of 1 billion is 40 million, and the higher one is used.
This is the fixed amount of the lower level. The rights of people are in the upper level.
This does not match the calculation of this level.
cards.answer: 40 million
cards.explanation: The rights of people are in the upper level: 20 million or 4%. Here 4% of 1 billion is 40 million, which is more than 20 million.

cards.question: A company has a worldwide revenue of 100 million. It fails its duties as a processor under Article 25. What is the highest fine?
options: 2 million
20 million
10 million
4 million
options_why: This is 2% of 100 million. But the fixed amount of 10 million is higher, so it is used.
This is the fixed amount of the upper level. This duty is in the lower level.
This is 4% of 100 million, which is the wrong level.
cards.answer: 10 million
cards.explanation: Lower level: 10 million or 2%. Here 2% of 100 million is 2 million, which is less than 10 million. So 10 million is used.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a criterion for setting the amount of a GDPR fine?
options: The size of the office building of the company
How much the company cooperated with the authority
Whether the company reported the breach itself
The type of data that was affected
options_why: This is a criterion: cooperation.
This is a criterion: notification.
This is a criterion: data type.
cards.answer: The size of the office building of the company
cards.explanation: The criteria look at how serious the offense is and at the attitude of the company. The size of a building is not one of them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “GDPR Fines”.

cards.question: Two companies have a leak. One had protections, warned the authorities, and cooperated. The other hid the leak. Which statement is BEST?
options: Both companies will get the same fine
The first company will get a heavier fine because it had a leak
Only the company with the higher revenue will be fined
The second company will probably get a heavier fine
options_why: The criteria look at the attitude and the preparation of each company.
Preparation and cooperation count in its favor.
Both can be fined. Revenue only helps to calculate the maximum.
cards.answer: The second company will probably get a heavier fine
cards.explanation: Preventive measures, cooperation, and notification are criteria that lower a fine. Hiding a leak makes it worse.

cards.question: Which offense belongs to the upper level of GDPR fines?
options: Failing the duties of a certification body
Failing the duties of a monitoring body
Not respecting the rights of data subjects
Failing the duties of controllers and processors under Article 25
options_why: This offense is in the lower level.
This offense is in the lower level.
Articles 25 to 39 are in the lower level.
cards.answer: Not respecting the rights of data subjects
cards.explanation: The basic principles, the rights of people, and data transfers are in the upper level.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “GDPR Fines”.

cards.question: Which offense belongs to the lower level of GDPR fines?
options: Ignoring an order of a supervisory authority
Failing the duties of a certification body
Breaking the basic principles of processing
Transferring data to a third country without respecting the rules
options_why: This offense is in the upper level.
This offense is in the upper level.

cards.question: What is the highest amount of the lower level of GDPR fines?
cards.answer: Up to 10 million, or 2% of the worldwide annual revenue of the prior financial year, whichever is higher.

cards.question: What is the highest amount of the upper level of GDPR fines?

cards.question: Who administers GDPR fines?
cards.answer: The supervisory authorities of each member state.
